subtitle: Individual techniques are skills. A methodology is what makes you a professional.
briefing:
In 2019, a penetration testing firm sent two testers to a large regional bank — simultaneously, without coordination, as part of an internal methodology review.

The first tester opened his laptop, pulled up the scope document, and went straight to Nmap. Twenty-three minutes later, the bank's intrusion detection system flagged the scan. The engagement was suspended. The security operations team was paged. Three hours of incident response followed. The tester had not found a single vulnerability.

The second tester spent day one reading the scope document. She made a list of every in-scope domain. She ran WHOIS lookups on all of them. She built a DNS enumeration report. She ran Google Dorks for each domain. She checked Shodan. She checked the Wayback Machine. She searched GitHub for credential leaks. By end of day one she had a fourteen-page intelligence report. She had not touched a scanner. The bank's IDS had no record she had ever existed.

On day two, she began active testing. She already knew which systems were directly reachable (not behind CDN), which subdomains had older software, which login portals existed, and which API endpoints appeared unauthenticated. Her scanning was not random — it was targeted, based on what passive reconnaissance had already told her.

She completed the engagement in three and a half days. The first tester's engagement was restarted after a written apology and a revised plan. It took seven days and found fewer critical issues.

The difference between them was not skill. It was methodology.

This mission is about methodology.
whyItMatters: A professional penetration tester does not begin an engagement by running tools. They begin by understanding what they are looking for, what they are allowed to do, and what they already know — before making a single active request to the target. The passive reconnaissance phase, done properly, produces an intelligence picture that makes every subsequent phase faster, more targeted, and more effective. The methodology you learn in this mission is the framework used by professional testers at every major security consultancy in the world.
objectives: Describe the complete professional passive reconnaissance workflow from scope review to recon report
Explain how to plan a reconnaissance phase before beginning any information gathering
Combine WHOIS, DNS enumeration, and search engine reconnaissance into a single coherent intelligence profile
Prioritise an attack surface into Critical, High, Medium, and Low tiers based on passive findings
Identify when passive reconnaissance is complete and active testing can begin
Explain professional standards for scope, escalation, and immediate reporting of critical findings
skillsUnlocked: Planning a passive reconnaissance phase from a client scope document
Building a structured intelligence profile correlating WHOIS, DNS, and OSINT findings
Prioritising an attack surface by severity and exploitability
Making professional judgement calls on scope boundaries and escalation
closingMessage: The second tester's methodology had a name. She called it her playbook — the specific sequence she followed on every engagement, adapted to each client's scope. By the end of this mission, you will have your own. It will be built from everything you have learned across this module. And it will be the foundation for every technical skill you develop from here forward.
